opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd push back a little on the framing. I don't think every agent *has* to start with an explicit planning step. But for a lot of tasks it really helps, and the reason is fairly intuitive once you think about how these models work.

When a model jumps straight into acting, calling a tool or editing a file, it's committing to a direction token by token without stepping back to look at the whole problem. If it starts down the wrong path, every later step builds on that mistake, and errors compound over a long trajectory. Having it first lay out what it thinks the task is, what the pieces are, and roughly what order to do them in gives it a chance to catch misunderstandings before it's spent twenty tool calls going the wrong way.

It's a lot like how you'd want a junior engineer to work. You don't want them to open the codebase and start typing. You want them to spend a few minutes figuring out what they're actually trying to do. The model is in a similar position, except it has even less context than that engineer, because it's dropped into the problem cold.

There's also a practical benefit for the humans in the loop. A written plan makes the agent's intent legible. You can look at it and say, "No, that's not what I meant," or "You're missing this edge case," and correct it cheaply up front instead of after it's made a mess. That's a big deal for trust.

The caveat is that you don't want the plan to become a straitjacket. Agents learn things as they go: they read a file, a test fails, an API behaves differently than expected. A good agent treats the plan as a living document and revises it when reality disagrees. So I'd say: plan first, but stay flexible. And for really simple tasks, just let the model do the thing. Adding planning overhead there is just ceremony.

r001.rationale: The response describes planning before acting, but does not characterize it as an extended form of chain of thought.

r002.rationale: It says humans can correct the plan cheaply up front instead of waiting until the agent has made a mess, communicating a shorter feedback loop.

r003.rationale: The response says a written plan makes intent legible and supports trust, but does not say human approval makes the resulting work more auditable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way to put it is that planning is cheap and mistakes are expensive. When an agent just dives in and starts taking actions, it's doing a kind of greedy search. It looks at the current state, picks the next most plausible step, and commits to it. And that works fine for short tasks, but the moment you have something that's ten or twenty steps long, a bad decision in step two can send you down a path where you spend a huge amount of effort and tokens, and then you have to unwind all of it. Writing out a plan first forces the model to actually think about the whole shape of the problem before it touches anything.

The other thing is that language models are really good at critiquing and really good at the high-level reasoning, but if you ask them to do both the reasoning and the execution at the same time, they tend to get pulled into the weeds. You're reading a file, you're running a command, you see an error, and all of a sudden the error is the whole world and you've forgotten what you were originally trying to accomplish. Having a plan written down gives the agent something to come back to. It's an anchor. It can check in and say, okay, I've done steps one through three, I'm on step four, does what I'm seeing still make sense given where I'm trying to go?

And then honestly, the thing I underrated at first is the human-in-the-loop piece. If I'm using a coding agent and it tells me, here's how I'm going to approach this, I can look at that in thirty seconds and say, no, don't touch that module, or actually we already have a helper for that. That's a much cheaper point to intervene than after it's already written five hundred lines. So planning isn't just better for the model, it's a really natural handoff point for the person supervising it.

The caveat I'd give is that you don't want planning to be rigid. The plan should be a hypothesis, not a contract. Good agents update the plan when they learn something surprising. But starting with one, even a rough one, almost always beats starting with nothing.

r001.rationale: The response says planning makes the agent consider the problem’s overall shape, but does not characterize planning as an extended form of chain of thought.

r002.rationale: It says a person can review the plan in thirty seconds and intervene before the agent writes hundreds of lines, making intervention cheaper than reviewing the executed task.

r003.rationale: The response describes reviewing the plan as a handoff point for supervision, but does not state that approval makes the resulting work more auditable.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that an agent needs a chance to think about the whole task before it starts taking actions. If it jumps straight into writing code or calling tools, it can make a locally reasonable choice that takes it in the wrong direction, and then spend a lot of effort building on that choice.

A planning step gives it space to break the problem down, identify what information it’s missing, and decide how it’ll know it succeeded. It also gives the human a useful point to intervene: correcting a plan is much cheaper than correcting a finished implementation.

The plan shouldn’t be rigid, though. As the agent learns things, it should update it. The goal is to give its actions a coherent direction, while still letting it adapt.

sol-6.1.text:
I think planning is useful because an agent is making a whole sequence of decisions, and a mistake early on can send it pretty far in the wrong direction. If it jumps straight into taking actions, it can do a lot of work without checking whether that work actually serves the goal.

A planning step gives it a chance to break the task down, identify what information it needs, and decide how it will know it’s finished. It also gives you something to inspect: does the agent understand what you asked it to do?

But the plan should be provisional. You want the agent to act, learn something from the environment, and update the plan. The value isn’t that it can predict every step up front; it’s that it has a direction and a way to recognize when it needs to change course.

r001.rationale: The response describes planning as breaking down a task and setting direction, but does not characterize it as an extended form of chain of thought.

r002.rationale: It says a plan can be inspected and updated, but does not state that human iteration on the plan has a shorter feedback loop than iterating on the completed task.

r003.rationale: The response says a plan can be inspected, but does not mention human approval of an implementation plan or that approval making the work more auditable.
